overview.h1: HTS Chapter 11: Milling Products, Malt & Starches — Tariff Rates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 11: Milling Products, Malt & Starches — Tariff Rates & Import Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 51 HTS Chapter 11 tariff lines: wheat flour, corn and rice flour, semolina, rolled oats, potato flakes, malt, corn, potato and tapioca starch, inulin and wheat gluten. General, FTA and Column 2 rates plus the extra duty by country.

overview.intro:
Chapter 11 covers what mills, malt houses and starch plants make from grain, potatoes, pulses and roots: wheat and other flours, semolina and cornmeal, rolled oats, potato flakes, malt for brewers, native starches, inulin and wheat gluten. Its **51 tariff lines** carry small printed rates — 0.7¢/kg on wheat flour, 0.3¢/kg on malt, nothing at all on tapioca starch — with a few ad valorem exceptions: 6.8% on wheat gluten, 8.3% on chickpea and pea flour, 12.8% on mixed flours.

As with most farm goods, the extra duty by country decides the cost. Canada and Mexico supplied 52% of the $2.34B the U.S. imported in 2025, and USMCA-qualifying goods from both enter free. Goods from elsewhere pay the base rate **plus a Section 301 tariff** in force since July 24, 2026: 10% in total for the EU, +10% or +12.5% for most other large suppliers, +37.5% for China and Brazil. Five lines — cassava and other root flours, banana flour, cassava (tapioca) and other starches — are exempt from that duty for every country except China (see Rates by country).

productGroups.label: Wheat flour
productGroups.blurb: Wheat flour — bread, durum and pastry flours — carries one specific rate, 0.7¢/kg, on every line. On a $0.60/kg flour that is barely 1%; the extra duty by country is what moves the cost.

productGroups.label: Other cereal flours (corn, rice, rye, oat)
productGroups.blurb: Flours of other cereals. Corn, rice and rye flours pay fractions of a cent per kg and buckwheat flour is Free, but the residual line (oat, sorghum, barley flour) is 9% and blended cereal flours are 12.8%.

productGroups.label: Groats, meal & pellets (semolina, cornmeal)
productGroups.blurb: Groats, meal and pellets: semolina, cornmeal, grits and steel-cut pieces. Mostly cents per kg; groats and meal of other cereals are 9%, and cereal pellets are Free.

productGroups.label: Rolled, flaked & worked grains; cereal germ
productGroups.blurb: Rolled, flaked, hulled and pearled grains plus cereal germ. Rolled oats are 1.2¢/kg, barley flakes 2¢/kg, pearled barley 1.2% and wheat germ 4.5%.

productGroups.label: Potato flour, flakes & granules
productGroups.blurb: Potato flour and dehydrated potato flakes and granules — the base for instant mashed potatoes and snack doughs. 1.7¢/kg and 1.3¢/kg.

productGroups.label: Flours of pulses, roots & fruit
productGroups.blurb: Flours of pulses, roots and fruit. Chickpea, pea and lentil flour is 8.3% and most fruit and nut flours 9.6%; cassava and other root flours are Free and banana flour is 2.8%.

productGroups.label: Malt
productGroups.blurb: Malt for brewing and distilling. Unroasted (base and pale) malt is 0.3¢/kg and roasted (specialty) malt 0.42¢/kg — the chapter's biggest import by value.

productGroups.label: Starches & inulin
productGroups.blurb: Native (unmodified) starches and inulin. Wheat, corn and potato starch pay about half a cent per kg; cassava (tapioca) starch and other starches are Free; inulin is 2.6%. Modified starches are chapter 35, not here.

productGroups.label: Wheat gluten
productGroups.blurb: Wheat gluten (vital wheat gluten). 6.8% for food use, 1.8% when it will be used as animal feed — the widest gap in the chapter for the same product.

workedExamples.title: 20 tonnes of base malt from Saskatchewan
workedExamples.body: Unroasted malt is 0.3¢/kg: 20,000 kg × $0.003 = **$60** at the general rate. Malt made in Canada from barley qualifies under USMCA (milling or malting grain of chapter 10 into a chapter 11 product is the required tariff shift), so with a USMCA claim the duty is **$0** and the Section 301 duty does not apply (9903.05.93). Without a valid claim a $12,000 shipment would owe $60 + 10% = **$1,260**.

workedExamples.title: A container of vital wheat gluten from Australia
workedExamples.body: Wheat gluten for food is 6.8%, which the Australia FTA (SPI **AU**) makes Free. Australia is one of the 60 economies in the 2026 Section 301 action, so 12.5% is still added (9903.05.23): on a $45,000 container that is **$5,625**. The same gluten entered for animal feed (1109.00.10, 1.8%) pays the same 12.5%, because the FTA already removes the base rate.

workedExamples.title: 20 tonnes of Italian "00" flour
workedExamples.body: The general rate is 0.7¢/kg — $140 on 20,000 kg. For EU goods whose base rate is under 10%, the Section 301 action charges **10% of value in place of the base rate** (9903.05.39). On a $14,000 shipment the duty is **$1,400**, ten times the printed rate.

workedExamples.title: Tapioca starch from Thailand
workedExamples.body: Cassava (manioc) starch is Free at the general rate, and 1108.14.00 is on the Section 301 general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86), so the 12.5% Thai rate does not apply: **$0** duty. The same starch from China still pays the 25% List 3 duty (9903.88.03). Chemically modified tapioca starch is heading 3505, not this line.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) roasted malt put up as coffee substitutes (heading 0901 or 2101); (b) prepared flours, groats, meals or starches of heading 1901; (c) corn flakes or other products of heading 1904; (d) vegetables, prepared or preserved, of heading 2001, 2004 or 2005; (e) pharmaceutical products (chapter 30); or (f) starches having the character of perfumery, cosmetic or toilet preparations (chapter 33).

**Note 2.** Milling products of wheat, rye, barley, oats, corn, grain sorghum, rice and buckwheat belong in this chapter only if, by dry weight, their starch content is above 45% and their ash content is under a set limit (2.5% for wheat and rye, 3% barley, 5% oats, 2% corn and sorghum, 1.6% rice, 4% buckwheat); otherwise they are bran or residues of heading 2302. Germ of cereals always stays in heading 1104. Products that pass the sieve test (80% through a 315-micron sieve, or 90% through 500 microns for corn and sorghum) are flours of heading 1101 or 1102; the rest are groats, meal or worked grains of 1103 or 1104.

**Note 3.** For heading 1103, "groats" and "meal" are fragmented cereal grains of which at least 95% by weight passes a 2 mm sieve (corn) or a 1.25 mm sieve (other cereals).
notes.additionalUsNotes: **Additional U.S. Note 1.** Mixtures of products of headings 1101, 1102, 1103 or 1104 (other than mixtures of subheading 1102.90.30) are dutiable at **12.8%** (general), Free for AU, CL, E, IL, P and SG, and 20% (column 2), whatever the rates of the separate products.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 11: Milling Products, Malt & Starches — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 11 Flour, Malt & Starch Tariff Updates — What Changed Since January 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 11 (flour, malt, starches, wheat gluten) since January 2025: base rates on all 51 lines, the end of the IEEPA tariffs and the Section 122 surcharge, and the 2026 Section 301 tariffs by country, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). All 44 dutiable Chapter 11 base rates are the same in both; the only difference is that rolled and flaked oats (1104.12.00) now have separate statistical lines for certified organic and other oats, at the same 1.2¢/kg.

Everything else that changed came on top of the base rate. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada +35%, Mexico +25%, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**; China also keeps its 25% List 3 duty (**37.5%** in all) and Brazil adds the 25% Brazil Section 301 duty (**37.5%**). Five root-flour and starch lines are exempt from the 2026 action, and **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico pay nothing extra**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 11 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, China Section 301 List 3, the Nicaragua Section 301 phase-in, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 11 base-rate changes
changes.detail: 49 of 51 Chapter 11 lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. The other two are new statistical lines: rolled or flaked oats (1104.12.00) were split into certified organic (1104.12.00.10) and other (1104.12.00.90), both at the unchanged 1.2¢/kg.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 3 duties continue
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China Section 301 actions, so they did not terminate and stay in effect during the second four-year review. The 25% List 3 duty (9903.88.03) on every Chapter 11 subheading is unchanged.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties and import bans do not reach Chapter 11
changes.detail: Proclamations of September 8, 2026 moved some Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motor vehicles from the 50% Section 338 duty to an import ban from September 29, 2026. Malt and every other Chapter 11 line are on none of the lists (U.S. note 51, 9903.03.12–9903.03.14).

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties take effect; Chapter 11 not covered
changes.detail: 50% duties on certain Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy and motor vehicles (9903.03.12–9903.03.14) took effect after a 3-day suspension lapsed. No Chapter 11 line is on the lists in U.S. note 51.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover Chapter 11
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). EU goods pay 10% in total and Japan, South Korea and Switzerland 12.5% in total when the base rate is lower. Five Chapter 11 lines are on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86): 1106.20.90, 1106.30.20, 1108.14.00 and 1108.19.00. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94). FTA claims remove the base rate but not this duty.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). Its exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03) includes the same five root-flour and starch lines (1106.20.90, 1106.30.20, 1108.14.00, 1108.19.00). From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top for the other lines.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Four Chapter 11 subheadings were on the product exemption list (9903.03.03): 1106.20.90, 1106.30.20, 1108.14.00 and 1108.19.00. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil, India and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75) renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025. AGOA (SPI D) makes every dutiable Chapter 11 line Free for eligible sub-Saharan countries. GSP (SPI A, A*, A+), printed on most Chapter 11 lines, remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Nicaragua Section 301 tariff phases in from 2027
changes.detail: USTR's action on Nicaragua adds a duty on all Nicaraguan goods that do not originate under CAFTA-DR (9903.89.01): 0% in 2026, 10% from January 1, 2027 and 15% from January 1, 2028. It reaches every Chapter 11 line.

changes.title: Reciprocal-tariff exemption for four root-flour and starch lines
changes.detail: Executive Order 14360 widened the agricultural exemption from the reciprocal tariffs. Cassava and other root flours (1106.20.90), banana flour (1106.30.20), cassava starch (1108.14.00) and other starches (1108.19.00) are on the list in U.S. note 2(v)(iii)(a); the other Chapter 11 lines paid the reciprocal duties until they ended on February 24, 2026.

changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 11 goods fell from **$2.69B in 2024 to $2.34B in 2025** (-12.8%), after peaking at $2.92B in 2022. The drop was broad: rolled and worked oats and other grains (heading 1104) fell from $439M to $341M, wheat gluten from $369M to $286M, malt from $308M to $265M and potato flakes and flour from $105M to $73M. Starches and inulin, the largest heading, edged up to $516M.

Canada is the anchor supplier — **$940M, 40% of the total** — shipping rolled oats, malt, wheat flour, semolina and oat groats. Mexico ($273M) sends mostly corn flour. The rest is specialised: native starches from Thailand (cassava), Germany, Denmark, Belgium and the Netherlands; wheat gluten from Australia ($142M), Germany and Lithuania; Italian wheat flour; and German and British specialty malt.

Through 2025 USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico paid no extra duty, while most other suppliers paid the IEEPA reciprocal tariff from April 2025 — 10% or more on top of small base rates. Those duties ended on February 24, 2026; since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5% applies instead. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on flour, malt and starch depends far more on **where it comes from** than on what it is. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — computed from the current tariff schedule with the same engine as the tariff calculator.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free**, **EU goods pay 10%** in place of the base rate, Australia and Chile keep their FTA's Free base rate but add 12.5%, and **China pays 37.5%** on top. Cassava starch, other starches and root and banana flours are exempt from the 2026 action for every listed country except China.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-11, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.
Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; AU for Australia; CL for Chile. GSP (A, A+) has lapsed and is not applied. Other preferences are not applied.
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.
EU: 9903.05.39 sets a 10% total when the base rate, or its ad valorem equivalent, is under 10% (U.S. note 52(k)). Mixed cereal flours (1102.90.30, 12.8%) are above 10% and pay only their base rate.
AGOA (SPI D) was reauthorized on February 3, 2026 through December 31, 2026; it would make the base rate Free for eligible sub-Saharan suppliers, none of which is in the matrix.

Entry also needs FDA prior notice and a registered foreign facility for every food line; wheat gluten and other vegetable proteins from China are detained under FDA Import Alert 99-29 unless lab results clear them (see Import documents).
industryAreas.exemptionCheck: Read U.S. notes 2, 20, 50, 51 and 52 to Chapter 99 subchapter III in the 2026 Revision 21. Four Chapter 11 subheadings — 1106.20.90, 1106.30.20, 1108.14.00 and 1108.19.00 — are on the Section 301 general exemption list (note 52(b), 9903.05.86), the Brazil exemption list (note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03), the Section 122 exemption list (9903.03.03) and the reciprocal agricultural exemption (note 2(v)(iii)(a)). No Chapter 11 code is on note 52(c)–(e), the country lists in note 52(j), or the Canada Section 338 lists (note 51). Every Chapter 11 subheading is on China Section 301 List 3 (note 20(f)); the only China exclusion that named a Chapter 11 product (dried pomegranate powder, 1106.30.4000) has expired.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 11: Milling Products, Malt & Starches — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Flour, Malt & Starch: FDA Rules, Documents & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 11) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The FDA, USDA and CBP rules for each HTS Chapter 11 line — prior notice, facility registration, FSVP, flour standards of identity, organic import certificates, the melamine import alert — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, FTAs, the feed line for wheat gluten, unmixed flours, drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Flour, malt and starch are food, so **FDA decides whether a shipment clears**: every line needs prior notice, a registered foreign facility and a U.S. importer that verifies its supplier, and flours sold under a standard name must meet their standard of identity. Wheat gluten from China is detained on arrival unless it is cleared for melamine.

The ways to pay less are in the schedule and the customs rules: claim **USMCA** on Canadian and Mexican goods (milling or malting grain into a chapter 11 product qualifies), claim an **FTA** where the base rate is the cost, enter **wheat gluten for feed** under its 1.8% line, ship flours **unmixed**, and claim **drawback** when the product is exported. Each depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The Section 301 duty — 10% of value for Canada or Mexico — plus the base rate
levers.appliesTo: All 51 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, in any format (it can be on the invoice). The Chapter 11 rule of origin is a change from any other chapter: flour, malt, starch or gluten made in Canada or Mexico from grain, potatoes or roots of any origin qualifies; blending or repacking imported flour does not.
levers.caveat: Claiming without a valid certification exposes the entry to the 10% Section 301 duty plus penalties. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim the FTA or AGOA rate where the base rate is the cost
levers.saves: The base rate: up to 9.6% (fruit and nut flours), 8.3% (pulse flours), 6.8% (wheat gluten) or 12.8% (mixed flours)
levers.appliesTo: Every dutiable line for goods of Australia, Chile, Korea, Israel, Singapore, Colombia, Peru, Panama, CAFTA-DR, Morocco, Bahrain, Oman, Jordan, and AGOA countries (through December 31, 2026)
levers.document: Proof of origin under the agreement and the SPI on the entry line (AU, CL, KR, …, D for AGOA).
levers.caveat: FTA claims do not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)), and for Korea the 12.5% Section 301 rate replaces the base rate anyway. GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020, so a GSP claim pays the general rate.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Enter wheat gluten for animal feed under 1109.00.10
levers.saves: 5 points of base rate: 1.8% instead of 6.8% — $2,250 on a $45,000 container
levers.appliesTo: Wheat gluten that will be used as animal feed (1109.00.10.00)
levers.document: This is an actual-use line: the use must be intended at import, the gluten must be used as feed, and proof of use (a certificate from the end user describing the use) must be filed within 3 years of entry.
levers.caveat: If proof of use is not filed, CBP liquidates at the 6.8% food rate. Any Section 301 duty for the country still applies.

levers.title: Import flours and meals separately rather than pre-mixed
levers.saves: A blend of products of headings 1101–1104 is 12.8% (Additional U.S. Note 1), against 0.7¢/kg for wheat flour, 0.3¢/kg for corn flour or 1.2¢/kg for rolled oats on their own
levers.appliesTo: Mixed cereal flours, groats and flakes (1102.90.30 and other mixtures of headings 1101–1104)
levers.document: Commercial invoices and product specifications that show each flour as a separate product; blend in the United States.
levers.caveat: Prepared mixes with leavening, sugar or fat are heading 1901, not chapter 11. The EU 10% total applies either way for EU goods under 10% base.

levers.title: Claim drawback when the product, or what it is made into, is exported
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid on imported malt, flour or starch used to make goods that are exported (for example malt brewed into exported beer)
levers.appliesTo: All lines, when the imported goods or substitutes are exported or used in manufacturing exported goods
levers.document: A drawback claim filed in ACE within 5 years of import, with records linking the import to the export.
levers.caveat: Drawback needs set-up (a manufacturing ruling for manufacturing claims) and only refunds duties actually paid.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification (flour vs. meal, native vs. modified starch, chapter 11 vs. 1901) before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its composition and the milling or sieve data.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different product may need its own.

rules.title: Prior notice of every food shipment, confirmed before arrival (at least 2 hours by road, 4 by rail or air, 8 by water)
The foreign mill, malt house or starch plant must be registered with FDA as a food facility
Foreign Supplier Verification Program: the U.S. importer must assess hazards and verify each foreign supplier
Food labeling: name, ingredients, net quantity, nutrition facts and the wheat allergen declaration
Standards of identity: flour, enriched flour, whole wheat and durum flour, corn flour and meal, farina and semolina sold under those names must meet 21 CFR part 137
China: wheat gluten and other vegetable proteins are detained without examination for melamine (Import Alert 99-29) unless the firm is on the green list or a LAAF-accredited lab clears the lot
Animal feed: wheat gluten and cereal pellets for feed fall under FDA's animal food rules (and FSVP for animal food)
Certified organic lines: each shipment needs NOP Import Certificate data in ACE (required since March 19, 2024)
Packaging: wood pallets and crates must be ISPM 15 treated and marked; used jute or burlap bags from khapra beetle countries are regulated

groups.label: Wheat flour
groups.note: Flour sold as "flour", "enriched flour", "whole wheat flour" or "durum flour" must meet its FDA standard of identity (21 CFR part 137); organic lines need an NOP import certificate.

groups.label: Other cereal flours (corn, rice, rye, oat)
groups.note: Corn and rice flours are covered by the same FDA food rules; mixed cereal flours are 12.8% (subheading 1102.90.30).

groups.label: Groats, meal & pellets (semolina, cornmeal)
groups.note: Semolina, farina and corn meals have FDA standards of identity (21 CFR part 137).

groups.label: Rolled, flaked & worked grains; cereal germ
groups.note: Organic rolled oats (1104.12.00.10) need an NOP import certificate.

groups.label: Malt
groups.note: Malt is a food ingredient for FDA purposes: brewers and distillers that import it are the FSVP importer unless another U.S. owner is named.

groups.label: Starches & inulin
groups.note: Native starches only — chemically modified starches, dextrins and starch glues are heading 3505.

groups.label: Wheat gluten
groups.note: Vital wheat gluten from China is on FDA Import Alert 99-29 (melamine). The 1.8% feed line is an actual-use provision.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations — not legal advice. FDA import alerts and agency requirements change; check them before each shipment.

seo.title: Flour, Malt & Starch Tariffs FAQ: HS Codes, Italian Flour, Canadian Oats, Tapioca Starch (HTS Ch. 11) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about Chapter 11 imports: HS codes for wheat flour, semolina, malt, corn, potato and tapioca starch, wheat gluten and rolled oats, and the tariff on Italian flour, Canadian oats and malt in 2026.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing flour, oats, malt, starch and wheat gluten into the U.S. — HS codes, tariffs by country and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: USMCA-qualifying flour, oats, malt and starch from Canada and Mexico enter free — no base rate, no extra duty. Canada and Mexico supplied 52% of 2025 imports.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty is a Section 301 tariff: 10% in total for the EU, +10% or +12.5% for most other suppliers, 37.5% in all for China and Brazil.
Cassava (tapioca) starch, other native starches and root and banana flours are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty for every country except China.
FDA rules apply to every line: prior notice, a registered foreign facility, FSVP, and for Chinese wheat gluten the melamine import alert.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for wheat flour?
searchedAs: hs code for whole wheat flour
hs code for durum wheat flour
hs code of atta wheat flour
faqs.answer: 1101.00 (wheat or meslin flour). The U.S. splits it into 10-digit lines by wheat type: 1101.00.00.10 hard spring, .20 durum, .30 white winter, .50 certified organic and .60 other — whole wheat flour and atta included. Every line is 0.7¢/kg at the general rate and Free under USMCA and the FTAs. Semolina is not flour: it is 1103.11.00.20. Flour mixes with leavening or other ingredients are heading 1901.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on Italian flour?
faqs.answer: Yes: 10% of the flour's value since July 24, 2026. For EU goods whose base rate is under 10%, the Section 301 action charges 10% in place of the base rate (9903.05.39), and wheat flour's base rate is 0.7¢/kg. Before that, the 15% EU reciprocal rate applied until February 24, 2026, then the 10% Section 122 surcharge until July 23, 2026. The U.S. imported $50M of wheat flour from Italy in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for semolina?
faqs.answer: Wheat semolina is 1103.11.00.20 (0.5¢/kg); other wheat groats and meal, such as farina, are 1103.11.00.40. Corn semolina, grits and cornmeal are 1103.13 (0.3¢/kg). Semolina sold under that name must meet FDA's standard of identity (21 CFR 137.320).

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for malt?
faqs.answer: Malt is heading 1107: 1107.10.00.00 for unroasted (base) malt at 0.3¢/kg and 1107.20.00.00 for roasted malt at 0.42¢/kg. Malt extract is 1901.90 and malt drinks are chapter 22, not here. Canada supplied $193M of the $265M of malt imported in 2025; USMCA-qualifying Canadian malt is Free with no extra duty, and the 2026 Canada Section 338 measures on alcoholic beverages do not cover malt. German malt pays 10% in total, British malt 0.3¢/kg plus 10%.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on oats, flour and malt from Canada?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on imports from canada
faqs.answer: Not on goods that qualify for USMCA, which most Canadian milling products do — milling or malting grain into a chapter 11 product meets the rule of origin. USMCA-qualifying goods pay no base rate and are exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian products (9903.05.93). Goods that don't qualify pay the base rate (1.2¢/kg for rolled oats) plus 10% (9903.05.29). The 35% IEEPA duty ended February 24, 2026. Canada shipped $302M of rolled and worked grains, mostly oats, in 2025. Whole oats are chapter 10, not here.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for corn starch?
faqs.answer: Native corn (maize) starch is 1108.12.00 — .10 for food use and .90 for other uses — at 0.54¢/kg. Modified corn starch, dextrins and starch glues are heading 3505 in chapter 35, not chapter 11. Corn flour is 1102.20 and cornmeal 1103.13.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for tapioca (cassava) starch?
searchedAs: hs code for modified tapioca starch
faqs.answer: Native tapioca (cassava) starch is 1108.14.00.00, Free at the general rate. It is on the Section 301 general exemption list (9903.05.86), so suppliers such as Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia and Brazil pay no extra duty; China still pays the 25% List 3 duty. Cassava flour is 1106.20.90 (also Free and exempt). Modified tapioca starch is heading 3505. The U.S. imported $102M of cassava starch in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for potato starch and potato flakes?
faqs.answer: Potato starch is 1108.13.00 (.10 for human consumption, .90 other), at 0.56¢/kg; $169M was imported in 2025. Potato flour is 1105.10.00.00 (1.7¢/kg) and dehydrated potato flakes and granules 1105.20.00.00 (1.3¢/kg). From EU suppliers such as Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands all three pay 10% in total.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for vital wheat gluten?
faqs.answer: Heading 1109: 1109.00.90 for food and other uses (6.8%) and 1109.00.10 for gluten to be used as animal feed (1.8%, with proof of use within 3 years). Australia is the largest supplier ($142M of $286M in 2025): its FTA makes the base rate Free, but the 12.5% Section 301 duty applies. EU gluten pays 10% in total. Gluten from China pays 6.8% + 37.5% and is detained under FDA Import Alert 99-29 unless lab results clear it of melamine.

faqs.question: What are the HS codes for rice flour and corn flour?
faqs.answer: Rice flour is 1102.90.25.00 (0.09¢/kg) and corn flour 1102.20.00.00 (0.3¢/kg); cornmeal is 1103.13.00.20 (0.3¢/kg). Mexico is the largest supplier of non-wheat flours ($185M in 2025), and USMCA-qualifying Mexican corn flour enters free. Oat, barley and sorghum flours fall in the residual line 1102.90.60 at 9%.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for rolled oats?
faqs.answer: Rolled or flaked oats are 1104.12.00 at 1.2¢/kg, split into 1104.12.00.10 (certified organic) and 1104.12.00.90 (other). Hulled, cut or otherwise worked oats are 1104.22.00.00 (0.5%) and oat groats and meal 1103.19.12.00 (0.8¢/kg). Whole oats are 1004 in chapter 10. Organic shipments need NOP Import Certificate data in ACE.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for inulin?
faqs.answer: 1108.20.00.00, at 2.6% general (Free under USMCA and the FTAs). The U.S. imported $94M of inulin in 2025. EU inulin pays 10% in total under the 2026 Section 301 action; inulin from other Section 301 economies pays 2.6% plus 10% or 12.5%.

faqs.question: What does HS code 1108 cover?
faqs.answer: Native starches and inulin: 1108.11 wheat starch (0.54¢/kg), 1108.12 corn starch (0.54¢/kg), 1108.13 potato starch (0.56¢/kg), 1108.14 cassava starch (Free), 1108.19 other starches such as rice starch (Free) and 1108.20 inulin (2.6%). Starches and inulin were the largest Chapter 11 import group in 2025, $516M.

faqs.question: How much flour, malt and starch does the U.S. import?
faqs.answer: $2.34B of Chapter 11 goods in 2025, down 12.8% from $2.69B in 2024. Starches and inulin ($516M), rolled and worked grains ($341M), wheat flour ($305M), wheat gluten ($286M) and malt ($265M) were the largest groups. Canada supplied 40%, Mexico 12% and Germany 7.5%.
